topic.subject: science
topic.title: Light, shadows and reflections
topic.scope: luminous and non-luminous objects, transparent/translucent/opaque, how shadows form, light travels in straight lines, pinhole camera

misconceptions.statement: We see objects because our eyes send out rays of light to touch them.
misconceptions.why: Students feel that vision is an active process directed by the observer.
misconceptions.fix: We see objects only when light from a source falls on them and then travels to our eyes.

probe.question: Can you see a book in a room that is completely dark?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if I open my eyes wide enough.

misconceptions.root_belief: perception is an active outward process
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's research on children's ideas

misconceptions.statement: The Moon is a luminous object because it glows brightly at night.
misconceptions.why: The Moon appears to be a source of light in the night sky.
misconceptions.fix: The Moon is non-luminous; it only reflects the light of the Sun that falls on it.

probe.question: Why does the Moon shine?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it produces its own light like a bulb.

misconceptions.statement: Transparent objects like clear glass do not reflect any light and are invisible.
misconceptions.why: Because light passes through them, students think they have no interaction with light.
misconceptions.fix: Even transparent objects reflect a small amount of light, which is why we can see the surface of glass.

probe.question: Why can you see a glass window even though it is clear?
probe.wrong_answer: You can't see the glass, you only see the frame.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Light can bend around corners to reach the other side of a wall.
misconceptions.why: Students observe that a room gets bright even if the bulb is in the hallway.
misconceptions.fix: Light only travels in straight lines; it reaches other areas by reflecting off walls and floors.

probe.question: If you look through a bent pipe at a candle, will you see the flame?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because light flows through the pipe.

misconceptions.statement: A shadow is a physical thing or a reflection that exists on its own.
misconceptions.why: Shadows move with the person, making them seem like an attached property or object.
misconceptions.fix: A shadow is simply the absence of light in a region where an opaque object blocked it.

probe.question: What is a shadow made of?
probe.wrong_answer: It is made of black air or a dark reflection.

misconceptions.statement: Shadows can be seen even if there is no screen or surface behind the object.
misconceptions.why: Students think the shadow is 'cast' into the air.
misconceptions.fix: A shadow can only be seen when it falls on a surface like the ground, a wall, or a screen.

probe.question: If you hold a bird in the high sky, will you see its shadow on the ground?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the shadow stays right under the bird in the air.

misconceptions.statement: The image in a pinhole camera is upright because light goes straight through the hole.
misconceptions.why: Students assume the image must look exactly like the object in orientation.
misconceptions.fix: Light from the top of the object travels in a straight line through the pinhole to the bottom of the screen, creating an inverted image.

probe.question: What happens to the image of a candle in a pinhole camera?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays upright because the hole is too small to flip it.

misconceptions.root_belief: images must look like the object

misconceptions.statement: Only mirrors and very shiny metals reflect light.
misconceptions.why: Students associate 'reflection' only with seeing a clear image of themselves.
misconceptions.fix: All objects we see reflect light; mirrors reflect it in a way that forms an image, while others scatter it.

probe.question: Does a piece of white paper reflect light?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because you cannot see your face in it.

misconceptions.statement: The shadow of an object is always the same size as the object itself.
misconceptions.why: Students often see their own shadows on the ground and assume a 1:1 size ratio.
misconceptions.fix: The size of a shadow changes depending on the distance between the light source, the object, and the screen.

probe.question: What happens to a shadow's size if you move the object closer to the torch?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays the same size as the object.

misconceptions.root_belief: size is an intrinsic fixed property

misconceptions.statement: Translucent materials block all light but are just 'weak' opaque objects.
misconceptions.why: Difficulty in distinguishing between 'partial' passage and 'no' passage of light.
misconceptions.fix: Translucent materials allow light to pass through them partially, but we cannot see clearly through them.

probe.question: Can light pass through a sheet of oiled paper?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is blocked because the paper is thick.

misconceptions.statement: A mirror image is just a person standing behind a transparent glass.
misconceptions.why: The depth perception in a mirror makes it look like there is space behind the glass.
misconceptions.fix: A mirror is an opaque object with a polished surface that reflects light back into the same room.

probe.question: Is a mirror transparent, translucent, or opaque?
probe.wrong_answer: Transparent, because you can see 'into' it.

misconceptions.root_belief: what is seen is physically there

misconceptions.statement: Light travels further at night than during the day.
misconceptions.why: Beams of light (like car headlights) are much more visible at night.
misconceptions.fix: Light travels the same way regardless of the time; it is just easier to see the contrast against a dark background.

probe.question: Does a torch beam go a longer distance at night?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the sun isn't there to stop it.
